Abstract 69

Background: 70

Dupilumab has been added to National Cancer Comprehensive Network (NCCN) 71

guidelines as a therapeutic strategy for managing certain cutaneous immune-related adverse 72

events (cirAEs) from immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. However, little is known about 73

the implications of dupilumab for cancer outcomes in this population. In this multi-institutional 74

study, we evaluate the impact of dupilumab treatment on survival among ICI recipients. 75

Methods: 76

We conducted a muti-institutional retrospective cohort study of ICI recipients from the 77

Mass General Brigham Healthcare System and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The dupilumab 78

group was compared to two control groups who did not receive dupilumab: with and without 79

cirAEs (control groups 1 and 2, respectively) that were 1:2 matched on sex, race, age at ICI 80

initiation, Charlson Comorbidity Score, year of ICI initiation, and ICI type. Manual chart review 81

was performed to obtain cirAE characteristics, systemic glucocorticoid use, dupilumab 82

treatment, vital status, and last contact date. Time-varying multivariable Cox proportional 83

hazards regressions were used to evaluate the impact of dupilumab on overall survival, adjusted 84

for sex, race, age at ICI initiation, ICI type, Charlson Comorbidity Index score, cancer type, 85

cancer stage at ICI initiation, and systemic glucocorticoid use. 86

Results: 87

A total of 53 cirAE patients treated with dupilumab were compared to two control groups 88

of 106 patients each. Most patients receiving dupilumab demonstrated either complete or partial 89

resolution of their cirAE (88.7%). In multivariable modeling, the overall survival of the 90

dupilumab group was not significantly different from control group 1 (HR=0.74, 95% CI:0.35- 91

1.60, p=0.5) or control group 2 (HR=0.70, 95% CI:0.32-1.51, p=0.4). However, the use of 92

Conclusions: 96

This study suggests that dupilumab is an effective therapeutic option for recalcitrant 97

cirAEs and does not adversely impact mortality. Due to the observed detrimental effects of 98

systemic glucocorticoid therapy, this study supports the need to shift away from systemic 99

glucocorticoid immunosuppression and towards targeted immune modulators for irAE 100

management that are less detrimental to ICI response. 101

• What this study adds: 119

This study concludes that dupilumab is an effective modality to treat cirAEs, with 88.7% of 120

patients responding to treatment. Additionally, this study demonstrates a 206-day average delay 121

from cirAE onset to dupilumab treatment suggesting the need for more timely consideration of 122

this therapeutic option. Finally, our results demonstrated that dupilumab does not increase 123

mortality among ICI recipients. 124

• How this study might affect research, practice or policy: 125

The results of this study suggest that use of dupilumab in the treatment of cirAEs is effective and 126

does not adversely impact mortality in the cancer population. Based on these findings, clinicians 127

should consider dupilumab treatment for cirAEs in the appropriate clinical setting. Moreover, 128

this study provides further evidence for the use of targeted immune modulators as preferred over 129

more commonly utilized broad-based glucocorticoid immunosuppression for the management of 130

immune related adverse events in the setting of ICI therapy. 131

Introduction 133

Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has revolutionized cancer treatment but is 134

associated with morbid and potentially life-threatening toxicities known as immune-related 135

adverse events (irAEs). Of these, cutaneous immune related adverse events (cirAEs) are the most 136

common, occurring in up to 40% of ICI recipients. Current National Cancer Comprehensive 137

Network (NCCN) version 1.2024 guidelines for the management of cirAEs of different 138

morphologies range from the use of topical steroids and oral antihistamines for low grade 139

eruptions to holding immunotherapy and initiating high dose systemic immunosuppressive 140

agents, typically systemic glucocorticoid therapy, for high grade eruptions.2 Though there is not 141

yet consensus regarding the use of systemic immunosuppression in patients receiving ICI 142

treatment for cancer care,3–5 there is a growing body of evidence suggesting that the use of 143

systemic glucocorticoids in ICI-treated patients is detrimental to survival outcomes,6,7 especially 144

early in the course of ICI therapy.8 In response to this concern, increasing attention has been 145

given to considering more targeted immune-modulating approaches for the management of 146

irAEs, which are hypothesized to be less likely to blunt the anti-tumor effect of ICIs than broader 147

systemic glucocorticoid immunosuppression. 148

Evidence of this approach notes the recent inclusion of dupilumab, currently approved by 149

the United States Food and Drug Administration for the management of atopic dermatitis and 150

prurigo nodularis, in the NCCN guidelines for the management of certain cirAEs. Dupilumab is a 151

monoclonal antibody that inhibits interleukin 4 (IL-4) and interleukin 13 (IL-13) cytokine 152

signaling and prevents the release of downstream immunoglobulin E (IgE), which plays an 153

important role in immune mediated allergic processes, primarily in the type 2 inflammatory 154

pathway.9,10 Though these guidelines propose the use of dupilumab for the management of 155

moderate to severe bullous eruptions and severe pruritus in the setting of ICI therapy,2 it has 156

However, though several recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of dupilumab in the 158

management of several specific morphologies of cirAEs, these have been limited to case 159

long-term follow-up to evaluate the specific impact of dupilumab on ICI outcomes. As a result, 161

there is no available data on the long-term impact of dupilumab on mortality among ICI 162

recipients. 163

In this multi-institutional retrospective cohort study, our primary aim is to evaluate 164

overall survival outcomes among ICI recipients treated with dupilumab. Our secondary aim 165

includes evaluating the efficacy of dupilumab in the management of cirAEs. To our knowledge, 166

this is the largest cohort of ICI recipients treated with dupilumab to date and the first to explicitly 167

evaluate survival outcomes by comparison to robust non-dupilumab treated comparator 168

populations of ICI recipients. 169

Methods 170

We conducted a muti-institutional retrospective cohort study of ICI recipients who 171

received dupilumab therapy for the management of cirAEs between September 27, 2017, and 172

December 08, 2023, at the Mass General Brigham Healthcare System and the Dana-Farber 173

Cancer Institute (MGBD). Figure 1 presents the population included in this study. We extracted 174

patient demographic and medical history information from the MGBD Research Patient Data 175

Registry17 and the Enterprise Data Warehouse18 using the same approaches as in our recently 176

published studies19–21 and in alignment with the published guidelines on defining cirAEs22. 177

Manual chart review was conducted to extract cirAE characteristics (cirAE status – yes or no, 178

cirAE onset date, cirAE morphology, and cirAE severity), dupilumab variables (dupilumab 179

status – yes or no, dupilumab indication, dupilumab start and end date, treatments before 180

Discussion 285

This multi-institutional retrospective cohort study suggests that dupilumab is an effective 286

treatment modality for recalcitrant cirAEs of various morphologies and that its use does not 287

adversely impact mortality among ICI recipients. Notably, the survival trend associated with 288

dupilumab was protective of mortality but did not reach statistical significance in this study due 289

to insufficient sample size of the dupilumab population to demonstrate this protective effect. 290

Interestingly, a recent study has suggested that dupilumab may enhance response to ICI 291

treatment in ICI-resistant cancers; in six patients with non-small cell lung cancer with 292

progressive disease while on PD-1 or PDL-1 receptor inhibiting immunotherapy, patients were 293

given adjunct dupilumab in addition to their continued ICI regimens.27 One of the six patients 294

experienced near complete response following addition of dupilumab.27 Similarly, though not 295

reaching statistical significance, our results suggest that the use of dupilumab for cirAE 296

management may be associated with a protective mechanism in the ICI population. Additional 297

studies with larger cohorts are necessary to further elucidate this potential relationship. Our study 298

demonstrates that dupilumab does not increase the risk of mortality in this population and adds 299

valuable data to aid oncologists and dermatologists in guiding their therapeutic selection and 300

therapy. Additionally, this is the largest study of dupilumab efficacy in the ICI-treated population 302

and the first study to explicitly explore its long-term safety profile in an ICI-treated population. 303

The utility of dupilumab in the management of cirAEs has previously been reported, and 304

our conclusions confirm these findings.1 Our results demonstrated an 88.7% response rate to 305

dupilumab therapy among ICI recipients across a broad range of cirAE morphologies, 306

demonstrating that this therapeutic strategy is highly effective. Prior studies have reported an 307

87% cirAE response rate to dupilumab use,1 which our findings independently validate in a 308

larger multi-institutional cohort. We also further stratified responders by cirAE morphology and 309

found that although dupilumab is effective for the management of multiple different 310

morphologies of cirAEs, its efficacy varies across morphologies. For instance, among individual 311

morphologies of cirAEs, dupilumab demonstrated the highest non-response for the management 312

of bullous eruptions and the highest complete response rate for the management of morbilliform 313

drug eruptions followed by eczematous eruptions. Interestingly, all patients with lichenoid and 314

other eruptions achieved partial or complete response with a 90% rate of complete response in 315

patients with mixed morphologies. As a result, this study suggests that the use of dupilumab in 316

the treatment of lichenoid, other, and mixed morphologies could also be useful and that 317

clinicians should consider broadening the indications for which they use dupilumab, despite the 318

current absence of these morphologies in the NCCN guidelines for the management of irAEs.2 319

Additionally, these results confirm that the use of high dose systemic glucocorticoid 320

immunosuppression within two years of immunotherapy initiation is associated with detrimental 321

effects on overall survival, which previous studies have also reported.6,28  Our findings also 322

indicate a significant delay from the time of dupilumab treated cirAE start to dupilumab 323

Our study suggests that dupilumab can be used in the management of treatment- 327

refractory cirAEs without impacting survival. Clinicians should consider using dupilumab in the 328

management cirAEs not responsive to topical therapies as a safer alternative to the more 329

commonly utilized systemic glucocorticoid immunosuppression and should counsel patients that 330

this therapeutic strategy does not adversely impact their ICI outcomes. Additionally, this study 331

demonstrates favorable response to dupilumab treatment across several cirAE morphologies, 332

including non-specific morphologies, and clinicians should discuss this treatment option with 333

their cirAE patients with difficult to classify rashes. This study provides further support for the 334

need to shift the paradigm of irAE management from reliance on systemic glucocorticoid 335

immunosuppression, which may dampen the desired immune response in the setting of ICI 336

treatment, toward more targeted forms of immune modulation, with the goal of uncoupling 337

toxicity from the therapeutic effect of ICIs. Additional studies exploring the use of other biologic 338

and targeted immunosuppressive treatment modalities for the management of cirAEs and irAEs 339

more broadly are necessary. 340

Limitations of this study include its retrospective nature and limited sample size of the 341

dupilumab-treated cohort. However, this is the largest study of dupilumab-treated cirAEs to date 342

and the first to include robust comparator cohorts to investigate the impact of dupilumab on 343

mortality in the ICI population. Future studies should confirm these findings among larger 344

cohorts of ICI recipients and investigate the optimal time, dosing, and frequency for dupilumab 345

therapeutic intervention in this population. 346

*Figure 1. The study population and data collection*

Legend: This study identified all ICI recipients who developed cirAEs and received Dupilumab for managing cirAEs as the case group (the dupilumab group). To demonstrate the robustness of this study, the dupilumab group was compared to two control groups that were identified using 1:2 matching based on sex, race, age at ICI initiation, Charlson Comorbidity Score, year of ICI start, and ICI type. The first control group included 106 ICI recipients who developed cirAEs and were not treated with Dupilumab; the second control group included 106 ICI recipients who did not experience cirAEs and were not treated with Dupilumab. ICI: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor; CirAE: Cutaneous immune-related adverse event.
